item.title: Ball Valves
item.description:
Where ball valves fit in a system

Ball valves are commonly selected when a line needs compact, fast on/off isolation. In corrosion-resistant piping systems, they are often considered for clean water, treated water, chemical feed lines, dosing skids, tank outlets, sample points, utility headers, and maintenance bypasses.

For most corrosive-service projects, a ball valve is not selected by the valve name alone. The body material, ball and stem design, seat material, seal set, end connection, pressure-temperature boundary, operating frequency, and actuator interface should all be reviewed against the actual duty.

item.title: Butterfly Valves
item.description:
Where butterfly valves fit in a system

Butterfly valves are often selected for larger pipe sizes where a compact, relatively lightweight valve is preferred for isolation or basic flow control. They are common in industrial water treatment, wastewater treatment, cooling water, utility headers, pretreatment systems, filtration lines, and selected chemical service where the liner, disc, and shaft materials match the duty.

Butterfly valves can be simple to install, but they are not simple to specify. The pipe standard, flange standard, valve style, liner material, disc material, shaft sealing, operating mode, and allowable leakage expectation should be reviewed before quotation.

item.title: Diaphragm Valves
item.description:
Where diaphragm valves fit in a system

Diaphragm valves are considered when the process fluid should be isolated from the operating mechanism, when the line contains corrosive chemicals or suspended solids, or when a replaceable diaphragm is preferred as a known wear component. They are often reviewed for chemical dosing, wastewater treatment, neutralization lines, slurry-like service, aggressive cleaning fluids, and selected throttling duties.

The valve is usually selected around the combination of body or lining material and diaphragm compound. The correct choice depends on media, concentration, temperature, pressure, vacuum exposure, solids, cycle frequency, and whether the valve is used for simple isolation or more frequent adjustment.

item.title: Check Valves
item.description:
Where check valves fit in a system

Check valves are installed where reverse flow could damage equipment, contaminate a line, drain a system, reduce metering accuracy, or disrupt process stability. They are common on pump discharge lines, chemical dosing systems, transfer lines, water treatment piping, wastewater equipment, and utility service.

A check valve should be selected around the actual flow condition, not only the pipe size. Flow velocity, cracking pressure, pressure drop, pump behavior, line orientation, solids, pulsation, and chemical compatibility can all affect performance.

item.title: Pressure Control & Chemfeed
item.description:
Where pressure control and chemfeed items fit in a system

Chemical dosing lines often need more than an isolation valve. Back pressure valves, relief valves, injection assemblies, calibration columns, pulsation dampeners, strainers, anti-siphon devices, tubing adapters, and pipe accessories may be required to make the system stable, maintainable, and reviewable.

These components should be selected around the metering pump and the actual injection point. Pump capacity, stroke behavior, suction arrangement, discharge pressure, injection pressure, chemical concentration, line size, connection type, and maintenance expectations all affect the recommended package.

item.title: Actuators
item.description:
Where actuators fit in a valve package

Actuators convert manual valves into remotely operated or automated valve packages. They are commonly used on ball valves, butterfly valves, diaphragm valves, and selected pressure control or process assemblies where the plant needs remote open/close operation, interlock, sequencing, feedback, or modulating control.

Actuator selection should begin with the valve and duty. A valve that operates easily by hand may still require a larger actuator because of pressure differential, seat load, media behavior, temperature, cycle frequency, or safety factor requirements.

item.title: Fittings
item.description:
Where fittings fit in a piping package

Fittings connect valves, pumps, tanks, dosing accessories, instruments, and piping into a workable system. In corrosion-resistant projects, installation problems often come from mismatched pipe standards, connection methods, gasket materials, flange drilling, thread standards, or missing adapters rather than from the valve body itself.

Fittings should be reviewed as part of the complete piping package. The material, pressure rating, temperature boundary, chemical exposure, installation method, maintenance access, and document requirements should match the valve and pipe system.
